patient.chief_complaint: Recurrent syncope, progressive slowing of movement, and balance difficulties over 18 months
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Daniel Kowalczyk is a 62-year-old right-handed retired electrical engineer who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic for evaluation of recurrent syncopal episodes, progressive motor slowing, and gait instability that have evolved over the past eighteen months. His medical history is notable for Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome diagnosed at age 42 after a witnessed syncopal episode with documented delta waves on ECG, which was managed conservatively as he remained asymptomatic for over fifteen years. Eight months ago, he experienced a syncopal episode while standing in his garage workshop, falling backward and striking his occiput on a workbench. He was evaluated in the emergency department where an ECG again demonstrated the known WPW pattern, and the event was attributed to a possible re-entrant tachycardia. A second syncopal episode occurred four months later while standing from a seated position at a restaurant, and was similarly attributed to his WPW by his cardiologist. However, his wife has become increasingly concerned about changes beyond the syncope. She reports that over the past eighteen months, his movements have become noticeably slower and more deliberate. He now takes considerably longer to dress in the morning, struggles with buttons and zippers, and his handwriting has become progressively smaller and harder to read. His walking pace has diminished markedly, and she has noticed that he no longer swings his arms naturally when walking. He has had three near-falls, all with a tendency to topple backward, though he has managed to catch himself or grab nearby support. His chronic constipation, present for approximately three years, has worsened significantly despite daily polyethylene glycol, and he sometimes goes four to five days without a bowel movement. His erectile dysfunction preceded the motor symptoms by approximately one year. Three years ago, his wife began sleeping in a separate bedroom because he was thrashing, kicking, and shouting during sleep, sometimes enacting what appeared to be fighting or running in his dreams. A sleep study confirmed REM sleep behavior disorder. He reports mild difficulty with multitasking at work, which contributed to his early retirement six months ago. He has noticed he cannot smell his morning coffee anymore and initially attributed this to aging. He denies visual hallucinations. He has not been exposed to neuroleptics, metoclopramide, or other dopamine-blocking agents. The referring cardiologist has been focused on the WPW syndrome as the explanation for his syncopal episodes, but his wife specifically requested a neurology referral because she feels the motor and balance changes are a separate and worsening problem.

results.title: Orthostatic Hypotension in Parkinson's Disease: Frequency, Clinical Correlates, and Impact on Daily Living
results.summary: Orthostatic hypotension occurs in 30-58% of PD patients and is associated with disease severity. Syncope due to OH should be differentiated from cardiac syncope.

results.title: Distinguishing Cardiac Syncope from Orthostatic Syncope in the Neurology Clinic
results.summary: Positional nature of syncope (occurring on standing), absence of palpitations, and blunted heart rate response favor neurogenic orthostatic hypotension over cardiac arrhythmia. Co-existing cardiac conduction abnormalities (such as WPW) can mislead clinicians.

results.title: REM Sleep Behavior Disorder as a Prodromal Marker for Alpha-Synucleinopathies
results.summary: Isolated RBD converts to PD, DLB, or MSA at rates of 6-7% per year. When combined with hyposmia, constipation, and subtle motor signs, specificity for alpha-synucleinopathy exceeds 90%.

output.summary: Orthostatic hypotension-related syncope is common in Parkinson's disease and should be distinguished from cardiac arrhythmia-related syncope, even in patients with known conduction abnormalities like WPW. The positional nature of episodes and blunted heart rate response favor autonomic dysfunction. RBD is a highly specific prodromal marker for alpha-synucleinopathies.

critical_actions: Apply MDS 2015 clinical diagnostic criteria for Parkinson's disease (bradykinesia plus rest tremor or rigidity, supportive features, no absolute exclusion criteria)
Document temporal sequence of motor and non-motor (REM sleep behavior disorder, hyposmia, constipation, orthostatic intolerance) features
Review the full medication list for dopamine receptor antagonists (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, antipsychotics) and any other agents that can mimic or worsen parkinsonism
Co-manage syncope with cardiology to address WPW contribution
Treat orthostatic hypotension non-pharmacologically first, then midodrine, droxidopa, or fludrocortisone as needed
Document baseline cognition for surveillance of PDD/DLB conversion
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, or promethazine for nausea in a patient with parkinsonism

Do not prescribe typical antipsychotics (haloperidol, fluphenazine) or most atypical antipsychotics (risperidone, olanzapine, aripiprazole) — restrict pharmacotherapy of psychosis to quetiapine, clozapine, or pimavanserin
Do not prescribe centrally acting anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine) in older adults or in any patient with cognitive impairment
Avoid agents that worsen orthostatic hypotension unless cardiologic indication outweighs

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle due to the co-existing WPW syndrome serving as a major red herring for syncope etiology. The known cardiac conduction abnormality (confirmed on ECG with delta waves) plausibly explains the syncopal episodes, potentially diverting the agent from recognizing the orthostatic mechanism and the broader constellation of prodromal alpha-synucleinopathy features. Additionally, the relatively symmetric parkinsonism and early autonomic dysfunction raise the differential of MSA-P versus PD, requiring integration of orthostatic measurements, levodopa response, and longitudinal clinical features.
